title: Folio 4: The Judge Who Lied to Save a Life
description: A man sits blindfolded on the executioner's mat, and the sword is already drawn. In the middle of the night, the chief judge of the Abbasid empire rides to stop it, armed with nothing but words. This is the story of Afshin, Bu Dulaf and Ahmad ibn Abi Duwad, as Beyhaqi tells it.
source: Tarikh-e Beyhaqi, the story of Afshin and the deliverance of Bu Dulaf (told before the hanging of Hasanak, after Ismail ibn Shihab from Ahmad ibn Abi Duwad); with standard scholarship for Afshin's background and his trial and death (840-841 CE)
cold_open: Midnight, in the city of the caliphs. A man sits on the executioner's mat, his eyes bound, a drawn sword beside him. Across the city, an old judge wakes from his sleep, and cannot say why his heart is so heavy.

extra_shorts.from: And here the judge made a choice
extra_shorts.hook: He lied in the caliph's name to stop an execution
The caliph's answer saved two lives

paragraphs: Welcome to The Honest Historian. I'm Mehdi Rahmani, and this is Folio Four. Imagine a man sitting on a leather mat, his eyes bound with a cloth. Beside him stands an executioner with a drawn sword. And somewhere in the dark streets of the city, an old judge is riding as fast as he can, without knowing yet why.
Today, we leave the court of Ghazni for a while. We go back two hundred years, to the court of the caliphs, for a story that Beyhaqi thought worth saving.

First, a word about where this story sits. In the pages of Beyhaqi just before the hanging of Hasanak, the vizier we met in Folio One, Beyhaqi stops his own account and tells a tale from the distant past. He says he did not invent it. He heard it through a chain of tellers. A man named Ismail ibn Shihab said that he heard it from the judge himself, Ahmad ibn Abi Duwad.
So the voice we will hear, in my retelling, is the voice of that judge, speaking of a night he never forgot.
Why does Beyhaqi tell it? He says so plainly near the end. He writes these stories so that his readers may gain something from them.
Let me introduce the three men.

The first is the caliph, al-Mutasim. He was the ruler of the Abbasid empire, which stretched from North Africa to Central Asia. He reigned from the year eight hundred and thirty three to eight hundred and forty two. In those years his court sat at Samarra, a new city on the Tigris River, north of Baghdad.

The second is Afshin. That was a title, not a name. It was the old title of the princes of Ushrusana, a mountain land in Central Asia, near today's Tajikistan. This Afshin, whose own name was Khaydar, had become the caliph's greatest general. He had just won a long and bitter war against a rebel named Babak, in the mountains of Azerbaijan. And so, Beyhaqi tells us, the caliph honored him above everyone. He was proud, powerful, and feared.

The third is Bu Dulaf, whose full name was al-Qasim ibn Isa al-Ijli. He was an Arab nobleman, a commander, a governor in western Iran, and a famous patron of poets. He had served the caliphs for many years.
And between Afshin and Bu Dulaf, there was hatred. Beyhaqi calls it enmity and rivalry of the fiercest kind.

Then there is the fourth man, the one who tells the story. Ahmad ibn Abi Duwad was the chief judge of the empire. Beyhaqi tells us he was more powerful than any vizier, and that he served three caliphs, one after another. He was an Arab, a scholar, and a man whose word carried weight from east to west.
His story begins like this. One night, in the time of al-Mutasim, he woke up at midnight. He could not sleep. A strange gloom had settled on his heart, and he did not know why.

He called his servant, a man named Salama, and told him to saddle his mount. Salama was surprised. It is the middle of the night, he said. And the caliph has told everyone that he will not receive visitors tomorrow. Where are you going?
The judge lay down again. But he could not rest. So he got up, washed, dressed, and rode out into the dark, not even sure where he was going. He turned toward the palace.

At the palace gate, the chamberlain told him it was far too early. The caliph was alone, and wished to be left alone. But the judge insisted, and the chamberlain went in. He came back with a surprise. Come in, he said. You are expected.

The judge found al-Mutasim sitting alone, deep in thought. And the caliph said something that the judge remembered all his life. Why are you so late, he asked. I have been waiting for you for a long time.

Then the caliph explained. For months, Afshin had begged him to hand Bu Dulaf over to him, to take his wealth and to put him to death. Again and again, the caliph had refused. Bu Dulaf was a loyal servant with a long record. But the night before, worn down by Afshin's pleading, the caliph had made a slip. He had given in. Worse, he had bound himself with solemn oaths that he would not take Bu Dulaf back, and would not interfere.
And now, the caliph said, as soon as day comes, Afshin will kill him.
The caliph could not break his oath. But perhaps someone else could ask. Go to Afshin, he told the judge. Plead with him. Save the man if you can.

The judge rode as if his life depended on it. In his haste, his cloak slipped from his shoulders and fell in the road, and he did not even notice. He sent riders ahead to Bu Dulaf's house, afraid that he was already too late.
When he reached Afshin's house, the servants ran to meet him, as they always did, for he was a great man. He told his own men to wait at the door, and he went in.

Here is what he saw. At the far end of the courtyard sat Afshin. In front of him, a leather mat was spread on the ground. In that world, this was the mat on which men were executed, so that the blood would not stain the floor. On the mat sat Bu Dulaf, in nothing but his trousers, his eyes bound with a cloth. Beside him stood the executioner, with his sword drawn, waiting for one word.
Now comes the battle of this story. And it is not fought with swords.

Whenever the judge visited, Afshin would rise and bow so low that his head came to the judge's chest. This time, he did not move. His face turned yellow, then red. The veins stood out on his neck. He would not even look at his guest.

The judge did not take offense. He kissed Afshin, and sat down beside him. And then he began to talk. Anything, to keep Afshin's mind away from one word: strike. He even praised the Persians and the peoples of the east above his own people, the Arabs, because he knew this would please Afshin, who was proud of his ancient princely line. Later he confessed, with some shame, that this was a sin. But he said he did it to keep a man alive for a few more minutes.
Then he made his request. Grant me this man's life, he said, as a favor to me.
Afshin refused. The Commander of the Faithful has given him to me, he said, and he has sworn not to interfere.

So the judge humbled himself. He kissed Afshin's head. He kissed his shoulder. He kissed his hands. He bent down toward his knee. And Afshin, in Beyhaqi's account, told him coldly that a thousand kisses would do him no good.
And here the judge made a choice that could have cost him everything.

He drew himself up and reminded Afshin who he was. Then he said that he carried a message from the caliph himself. And the message, as Beyhaqi gives it, was this. Do not kill al-Qasim. Do not touch him. Send him home at once, because your hand is short of him. And if you kill him, I will have you put to death in his place.
There was no such message. The caliph had said nothing of the kind. The judge had just invented it, on the spot, in the caliph's name.
Afshin trembled. He went pale, and almost fainted. Is this truly the caliph's message, he asked.

The judge did not answer with words alone. He called in thirty or forty respected men, trusted witnesses from every quarter, and delivered the message again in front of them. Then he turned to the man on the mat and asked him, are you well? Are you wounded? And from behind the blindfold Bu Dulaf answered that he was unhurt. The witnesses saw it all.
Then the judge mounted and rode back to the palace, as fast as he had come.
He arrived sweating and out of breath. The caliph had a servant wipe his face, and asked him what had happened. And the judge began to tell him everything.
He had just reached the part about the thousand kisses when the door opened, and in walked Afshin himself.
Think about the judge's fear in that moment. If Afshin told the caliph about the message, and the caliph denied it, then the judge would be shamed as a liar, and Bu Dulaf would surely die.
Afshin spoke. Ahmad brought me a message from you, he said. Is it true that I may not kill him?
And the caliph answered. It is my message.

Then al-Mutasim reproached his general. Bu Dulaf was a servant of this house, he said. The better path would have been to set him free with honor. And then he added a line that is still quoted in Persian.
Har kasi aan konad ke az asl o gowhar-e vey sazad.
Everyone does what befits his root and his nature.
Afshin left, defeated.
When they were alone, the caliph turned to the judge. Why, he asked, did you deliver a message I never gave you?

The judge answered honestly. He said he could not bear to see a Muslim's blood spilled. He would accept whatever punishment came. And he believed that God would not hold him to account for a lie told to save a life.
And the caliph laughed. He approved of what the judge had done. Then he sent one of his own officers, with his own horse, to bring Bu Dulaf with honor to the judge's house.
When the judge came home, Bu Dulaf was waiting at his door. He threw himself at the judge's feet. The judge raised him up, embraced him, and told him to thank God, and the caliph.

Beyhaqi ends the tale simply. Anyone who reads this story, he writes, will understand what great men these were. They have all passed away, and what remains of them is their good name. And then, almost briskly, he says that he will now go back to his history.

Beyhaqi does not tell us what happened to Afshin. But other historians do. Not long after, the great general fell from favor. He was arrested, put on trial in front of the court, and accused of disloyalty and of secretly holding to the old faiths of his homeland. He died in prison, in the year eight hundred and forty one. Fortune, once again, had turned its face.

Why did Beyhaqi place this story here, just before the hanging of Hasanak? He does not say directly, so I will not put words in his mouth. But I notice this. In Hasanak's story, a man of power used his position to destroy an enemy, and nobody stopped it. In this story, a man of power used his position to save a life, at great risk to himself.
Beyhaqi lived among courtiers. He knew how easy it was to stay silent. I think he wanted his readers to see that it is never the only choice.
If there is one lesson here, it is this: a single brave word, at the right moment, can be worth more than a thousand kisses.

Next week, we come back to Ghazni, to meet the man who taught Beyhaqi everything he knew. Bu Nasr Moshkan was the master of the royal chancery, and he knew how a secretary survives at a dangerous court.

If you enjoyed this story, follow the show so you don't miss the next one, and share it with someone who loves history. I'm Mehdi Rahmani. This episode was retold from the Persian original of the History of Beyhaqi, and narrated with an AI rendering of my own voice. Thank you for listening.
